t: Introduction: OPCs and the problem of mortality
n: This lesson is devoted to poisoning with organophosphorus compounds, OPCs for short. OPCs are among the most effective insecticides and are widely used in agriculture and in the home. The same compounds have also been used as nerve agents: in the Syrian civil war, from 2013, and in the assassinations of 2017–2018. The main mechanism is that OPCs bind to the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, inhibit it and cause a cholinergic crisis. In Asia, OPCs account for most pesticide deaths. A common cause of death in hospital is respiratory failure, followed by cardiac arrest.

Now the global figures. More than 3 million severe acute poisonings are estimated to occur each year; unregistered cases are even more numerous. Annual mortality estimates are given by different sources and groups: Eddleston, in 2004, about 300,000; Ramadori, in 2023, 200–350 thousand. According to Worek, OPC mortality fell from over 258,000 in 2007 to about 110,000 in 2017. Attention: 300,000 refers to all pesticides, whereas 110,000 refers to OPCs only; do not mix these figures up. After the class I pesticides, parathion and mevinphos, were banned, deaths from OPC self-poisoning decreased.

t: Case fatality: developing and Western countries
n: The reasons for high case fatality are toxic substances, long transport distances, and a shortage of doctors and antidotes. Let us compare the figures. In developing countries case fatality is 10–20 per cent, and for some pesticides 50–70 per cent. In Western countries it is below 0.3 per cent. In acute OPC poisoning in hospital it is 15–23 per cent, and in India recently up to 33 per cent. In patients on mechanical ventilation mortality may exceed 50%. Remember: case fatality, that is, the proportion of those who die, is not the same as the number of deaths; these are different measures.

In developing countries, case fatality in self-poisoning is usually 10–20%, and for some pesticides reaches 50–70%. In Western countries, case fatality in self-poisoning from all causes is below 0.3%. That is, the difference is very large. The reasons are multifactorial: the high toxicity of locally available poisons, the long distance to take the patient to hospital, and the small number of medical staff. In addition, there is a lack of equipment, antidotes and staff training. There are also few proven methods for developing treatment protocols.

t: Case analysis: poisoning in a remote village
n: Case analysis. A patient who drank an OPC in a village was brought to hospital over a long distance. He is drenched in sweat, his pupils are pinpoint, and his breathing is laboured. Most poisonings occur far from hospital, where diagnostic methods are not easily found. According to some data, in developing countries patients die soon after admission. Therefore initial stabilisation is important. Question: list the factors that increased the risk of death. What will you check first in the emergency department: airway, breathing, circulation?

OPC groups: phosphates, phosphonates, phosphinates and phosphorothioates. They are very diverse in structure and toxicity. In agriculture, pesticides protect crops from insects, mites, nematodes, fungi, rodents, birds and weeds. Pesticides are also used in domestic and recreational settings; their use has spread not only in developing but also in developed countries. OPC poisoning has been recorded since the early 1950s, when they were introduced. Cases are frequent and have reached the scale of a social disaster.

t: Pesticides and nerve agents: the common mechanism
n: Organophosphorus compounds form part of effective insecticides, and some of them are military nerve agents. Both nerve agents such as sarin and VX, and pesticides, inhibit acetylcholinesterase. The degree of toxicity depends on the structure of the compound. OPCs were used in the Matsumoto attack in 1994 and the Tokyo attack in 1995, as weapons in Iraq and Syria, and in the assassinations in Kuala Lumpur and Salisbury. Sarin acts rapidly through mucous membranes, whereas VX acts with a delay, through the skin. In suicide, the pesticide enters mainly by mouth.

Mechanism of action. OPCs bind covalently to the serine in the active site of acetylcholinesterase. As a result, enzyme activity falls. If acetylcholine is not broken down, signal transmission continues and nervous function becomes overactivated. The chain is as follows: the OPC blocks the enzyme's serine, activity falls, acetylcholine accumulates, the synapse is overstimulated, and muscarinic and nicotinic signs appear. Signs: miosis, salivation and sweating, bradycardia, fasciculations and loss of consciousness.

t: Irreversibility of inhibition and enzyme recovery
n: According to Ramadori, inhibition is practically irreversible. He believes there is no drug that detaches the poison from the enzyme. The normal state is restored by synthesis of new enzyme in the liver, bone marrow and especially at synapses; the excess of acetylcholine may last for weeks. Attention: atropine is not a reactivator. It does not restore the enzyme; it only suppresses muscarinic signs and does not block the nicotinic effect. Oximes are supposed to remove the phosphyl residue from the enzyme. They cannot restore aged enzyme, and their benefit in human pesticide poisoning is debated.

Acetylcholinesterase blocked by an OPC may recover or age. Pralidoxime and obidoxime cannot restore aged enzyme. Let us look at the table. For soman, the ageing half-time is about 2 minutes, and the oxime is ineffective. For VR, that is, Russian VX, the ageing half-time is about 140 hours, so ageing is very slow. For G-agents, spontaneous reactivation is negligible; the enzyme does not recover by itself. For malaoxon, a dimethyl OPC, the reactivation half-time is 0.7 hours, which helps the action of the oxime. As examples of dimethyl OPCs, malathion and dimethoate are also given here.

The first quick question. Question: how do OPCs block acetylcholinesterase, and why does ageing with soman nullify the effect of the oxime? Student's answer: the OPC binds covalently to the active site. The enzyme blocked by soman ages in about 2 minutes, and the oxime cannot restore it. On epidemiology: in developing countries, case fatality in pesticide self-poisoning is usually 10–20%, and for some pesticides up to 50–70%. Attention: ageing and spontaneous reactivation are not the same thing. In one the enzyme does not respond to the oxime; in the other it recovers by itself.

Toxicokinetics: routes of entry. Sarin acts rapidly, within minutes, by inhalation and through mucous membranes. VX acts with a delay, within hours, through the skin. After ingestion, diazinon acts rapidly, whereas malathion and dimethoate act with a delay. Vapour pressure at 25 °C: sarin 2.9 mmHg, VX 0.0007 mmHg. VX is lipophilic and dangerous through the skin. After ingestion, P450 converts it to the oxon, paraoxonase detoxifies it, and lipophilicity retains it in fat. When VX enters through the skin, the peak in blood in animals is at 2–4 hours; the elimination half-life of sarin is less than 60 minutes.

t: Thions: conversion to the oxon and accumulation in fat
n: An organophosphorus compound of the thion type, that is, a pro-poison, is not active in itself; it becomes toxic by converting to the active oxon. Conversion of the thion to the oxon proceeds via the enzyme cytochrome P450 and affects the speed of onset of the poison's action. Fat-soluble OPCs such as fenthion are released slowly from fat depots into the blood over days and even weeks. The chain: the thion OPC is ingested, accumulates in fat depots, is converted by P450 to the active oxon, cholinesterase is blocked, and as it is released from fat the signs return.

t: Case analysis: a patient who drank fenthion
n: Case analysis. A patient arrived soon after drinking fenthion; there is no miosis or sweating, the lungs are clear, and cholinergic signs are not yet visible. Attention: the absence of signs does not mean safety. As the thion is activated and fenthion is released from fat, signs may appear later. If there are no signs, atropine is not needed now, but careful observation is essential; after stabilisation, review at least once an hour for the first 6 hours. Question: why may the initial mild picture be deceptive, and why is the risk of relapse high with fenthion?

t: Cholinergic syndrome: muscarinic and nicotinic signs
n: Cholinergic syndrome. Acetylcholine is not broken down; muscarinic and nicotinic receptors are excessively stimulated. Muscarinic signs: bronchorrhoea, bronchospasm, bradycardia, miosis, salivation and sweating. Atropine reduces them, whereas miosis resolves late. Nicotinic signs: fasciculations, muscle weakness, paralysis; atropine has no effect on them. Through nicotinic receptors a dangerous peripheral respiratory block may develop, and atropine cannot reverse it. Attention: bradycardia is not obligatory; the heart rate may be normal or even fast.

In daily assessment, five signs are used: miosis, profuse sweating, worsening air entry into the lungs, bradycardia and hypotension. In miosis the pupil is pinpoint. Profuse sweating indicates that atropine is needed. Bronchorrhoea is accompanied by bronchospasm and poor air entry into the lungs. Bradycardia is not always present. In hypotension, blood pressure falls. A severely ill patient is drenched in sweat with pinpoint pupils; miosis and sweat indicate that atropine is needed. Attention: bradycardia is not an obligatory sign; the heart rate may be normal or fast.

Poisoned patients are unstable: even mild poisoning can quickly become severe, and the patient's condition may deteriorate sharply. The authors did not use unvalidated severity scales. An initial low score may reassure the doctor; the international IPCS/EC/EAPCCT scale is used only retrospectively. The POP scale grades severity solely by clinical symptoms and is still considered practically useful. The central rule: emergency treatment is chosen by clinical signs, not by the name of the poison taken; tests are not performed at the bedside.

Intermediate syndrome. An early sign is weakness of the neck flexors: the patient has difficulty lifting the head from the pillow. Then the accessory respiratory muscles come into play, nasal flaring and tachypnoea appear, and cranial nerve palsies are added. Proximal weakness is observed, while distal strength is preserved. Not every patient with neck weakness develops the full syndrome, but they are at risk, so monitor them regularly.

The second quick question, about clinical features. Question: a patient is drenched in sweat, with pinpoint pupils, and breathing is laboured and wheezy. Does he need atropine? Answer: yes. Pinpoint pupils, that is, miosis, and profuse sweat point to an organophosphorus compound or carbamate, so atropine is needed. In assessing the need for atropine there are five signs: miosis, sweat, bronchorrhoea and bronchospasm, bradycardia, hypotension. Attention: the heart rate may slow, but a normal or fast rate is also common. Do not wait for bradycardia as an obligatory sign.

t: Case analysis: a patient with neck weakness
n: Case analysis. A patient poisoned with an OPC cannot lift his head from the pillow after initial care. What is the danger? Weakness of the neck flexors is an early sign of intermediate syndrome. Then the accessory respiratory muscles, nasal flaring, rapid breathing, sweating and cranial nerve palsies are added. In the limbs the proximal muscles weaken, while distal muscle strength is preserved. This means the patient is at risk of respiratory failure. Action: monitor the patient regularly, and measure respiratory volume and blood gases. Within agreed limits, carry out prophylactic sedation and intubation.

The order of first aid. First the airway, breathing and circulation are checked. If possible, give high-flow oxygen; keep the airway open with a Guedel airway. Left lateral position, head down: the risk of aspiration is reduced. In convulsions give diazepam intravenously at once. For monitoring, the Glasgow Coma Scale and a pulse oximeter are used. In an unconscious patient insert an endotracheal tube; most deaths are from respiratory failure.

t: The first 10 minutes: atropine and fluid
n: The first 10 minutes. Two venous lines are established: one for fluid and drugs, the other for atropine. Until atropine takes effect, 500–1000 ml, that is, 10–20 ml/kg, of normal saline is infused over 10–20 minutes. If the clinical picture is unclear, 0.6–1 mg of atropine is given; a rise in pulse of more than 20–25 and flushing of the skin indicate that there is no significant cholinergic poisoning. Pinpoint pupils and sweat in an area where pesticides are widespread are sufficient grounds for giving atropine; the test result is not awaited. Then reassess after 3–5 minutes.

Atropine loading and titration. In an unconscious patient, 1.8–3 mg of atropine is given rapidly intravenously, into a fast-running drip system. After 3–5 minutes the five signs are assessed. The goal: clear lungs, pulse above 80, systolic pressure above 80 mm Hg. Attention: if there is no response, do not repeat the previous dose; double it. Once atropinisation is achieved, switch to an infusion: 10–20% of the loading dose every hour.

Atropine acts within a few minutes; after 3–5 minutes five indicators are checked: air entry into the lungs, pressure, pulse, pupil and sweat. Steady improvement is needed in most indicators, not just one; the most important are lung auscultation, pulse and pressure. The goal: clear lungs, pulse above 80, systolic pressure above 80 mm Hg, dry skin and non-pinpoint pupils. Remember: it is not necessary to bring the pulse to 120–140; this indicates atropine toxicity.

After atropinisation an infusion is started: 10–20% of the total atropine used for loading, every hour. If a loading dose of more than 30 mg was needed, less is given; the infusion usually does not exceed 3–5 mg/hour. The five indicators are assessed about every 15 minutes; if atropinisation is lost, the bolus and infusion rate are increased. After stabilisation the patient is reviewed at least once an hour for the first 6 hours, then once every 2–3 hours, and watched for respiratory failure.

Signs of excess atropine: agitation, confusion, urinary retention, hyperthermia, intestinal paresis and tachycardia. If three signs, that is, confusion, fever and absent bowel sounds, are present together, the infusion is stopped and reviewed after 30 minutes. Once the signs have passed, the infusion is restarted at 70–80% of the previous rate; fever is actively cooled. Compare. With excess atropine sweating stops, whereas with OPC action there is profuse sweating. With excess atropine, tachycardia; with OPC action, bradycardia, sometimes normal.

Pralidoxime and obidoxime reactivate acetylcholinesterase inhibited by OPCs. Atropine suppresses only muscarinic signs; for respiratory block at nicotinic receptors an oxime is needed. However, the benefit is debated: the type of OPC, poison load, time of starting and dose limit it; in carbamate poisoning it is not recommended. Factors limiting the effect: in mega-dose poisoning, net reactivation is very small; with late starting, the enzyme has aged and the oxime has no effect; OPCs resistant to reactivation, for example soman, age quickly; in carbamate poisoning oximes are not recommended.

In OPC poisoning, gastric decontamination is considered once the patient is stabilised and, if necessary, intubated; it is not done immediately on admission. Gastric lavage is considered only if a highly toxic pesticide was drunk and the patient arrives within 1–2 hours. The patient must be calm and consenting, or intubated. Ipecac is contraindicated in pesticide poisoning. The effect of activated charcoal and gastric lavage is unknown; the clinical benefit of charcoal has not been proven. Attention: in an agitated patient, or a drowsy patient who is not intubated, gastric lavage can lead to severe complications, even death.

Case analysis. An atropine infusion has been started in a patient poisoned with an OPC. He is agitated, has a fever, and bowel sounds are inaudible. If confusion and fever occur with absent bowel sounds, atropine toxicity is suspected. The infusion is stopped, reassessed after 30 minutes, and then restarted at 70–80% of the previous rate. For agitation, diazepam 10 mg is given slowly intravenously, up to 30–40 mg per day. For fever, active cooling with a fan airflow and a damp towel. Question: why is it dangerous to tie an agitated patient to the bed? Answer: he struggles, generates heat, and hyperthermic cardiac arrest may occur.

t: Diazepam and haloperidol: why diazepam is chosen
n: In an agitated patient, diazepam 10 mg is given slowly intravenously and repeated if necessary; up to 30–40 mg per day. Diazepam is preferable to haloperidol: in those receiving atropine, a large dose of haloperidol may be required. Haloperidol is not a sedative, it disturbs central thermoregulation, prolongs the QT interval and increases the tendency to convulsions. Animal experiments have shown that diazepam may reduce damage to the central nervous system and central respiratory failure.

t: Causes of death: respiratory and cardiac failure
n: The most frequent cause of death is respiratory failure, followed by cardiac arrest, sepsis and hypovolaemic shock. At autopsy, interstitial oedema and haemorrhage are found in the lungs, and acute tubular necrosis in the kidneys. In-hospital mortality is 15–23%, in India 33%; in ventilated patients it may exceed 50%. The chain is as follows: acetylcholinesterase block, cholinergic crisis, hypovolaemia and pulmonary oedema, acute respiratory distress syndrome, that is, ARDS, and finally death with cardiac arrest.

Glandular hypersecretion, vomiting, diarrhoea and loss of urine rapidly reduce fluid volume. Hypotension may progress to hypovolaemic shock; oliguria and bradycardia resemble sepsis. Attention: shock is not sepsis. Signs of inflammation are often a consequence of tissue hypoperfusion. The chain: fluid loss, hypovolaemia and hypotension, oliguria and shock, tissue hypoperfusion, prerenal renal failure.

In those who died within the first 24 hours, interstitial oedema and haemorrhage were found in the lungs. These changes resemble acute respiratory distress syndrome, that is, ARDS; in the kidneys there is tubular necrosis. Acute tubular necrosis in the kidney is a sign of prerenal injury. In a mini-pig experiment, similar histological changes mimicked aspiration. As a result of aspiration, hospitalisation and death increase; there has been no progress in the last 25 years. Autopsy is carried out mainly to detect the poison; the mechanism of death is little studied.

The third quick question. Question: what is the most frequently cited cause of death in hospitalised patients poisoned with organophosphorus compounds? Answer: respiratory failure, followed by cardiac arrest, sepsis and hypovolaemic shock. Question: what autopsy finding is seen in the lungs? Answer: interstitial oedema and haemorrhage, resembling ARDS. Attention: in ventilated patients mortality may exceed 50%; in chlorpyrifos poisoning it was a risk factor.

Prognostic markers. Hypoalbuminaemia, especially together with a rise in C-reactive protein, that is, CRP, is considered a sign of poor prognosis. Lactate, blood pH, base deficit and APACHE II scores, that is, the disease severity scale, proved to be adverse factors. A rise in CRP is a sign of systemic ischaemia; lactate and base deficit indicate tissue hypoperfusion and the risk of death. Attention: BChE, that is, butyrylcholinesterase, is not a prognostic marker; it has mainly diagnostic value.

t: The Noh study: hypoalbuminaemia and mortality
n: The Noh study. 217 patients were analysed, aged over 18, arriving within 24 hours; in 40 the albumin was below 35 g/L. In hypoalbuminaemia, respiratory failure was seen in 100%, renal failure in 25% and hypotension in 55%. Results by group: in hypoalbuminaemia, mortality 45 per cent, cardiac arrest 32.5 per cent. In normoalbuminaemia, mortality 15.8 per cent, cardiac arrest 14.3 per cent. In hyperalbuminaemia, both mortality and cardiac arrest were 9.1 per cent. The authors could not find the cause of the hypoalbuminaemia; a sharp reduction in nutrition is possible.

t: Laboratory: value of BChE and AChE
n: Laboratory indicators. Activity is measured by a modified Ellman method; the half-life of BChE is about 24 hours. Individual differences are large, so a pre-poisoning value is needed for a final conclusion. If BChE activity is below normal, enzyme inhibition is possible, or synthesis in the liver may be reduced; therefore it is compared with the previous value. Attention: BChE and AChE activity did not correspond to the degree of involvement of cholinergic synapses, and is not a prognostic sign. Diagnostic value only.

t: Case analysis: a patient with severe acidosis
n: Case analysis. A patient drank about 200 ml of dichlorvos, that is, DDVP, an organophosphorus insecticide. Severe acidosis developed, and serum albumin fell to 1 g/dL. Treatment: 125 g of albumin, 6.5 litres of fluid and sodium bicarbonate were infused. This case was described as successful. The author's interpretation: the fall in albumin may have resulted from prolonged hypovolaemia. Therefore volume restoration was the mainstay. Question: why can restoring volume and albumin, and not only the antidote, save life? Discuss.

t: Conclusion: treat the patient, not the poison
n: Conclusion. Initial treatment begins with the standard sequence: airway, breathing, circulation. Since most deaths are from respiratory failure, respiratory protection and ventilation are important. Atropine is given to each patient in an individual dose. Gastric clearance is carried out only once the patient is fully stabilised, not immediately on admission. Hypovolaemia, hypoalbuminaemia, high lactate and CRP are secondary factors; correcting them may affect the outcome: treat the patient, not the poison. In hospital, mortality is 15–23%, and in ventilated patients it may be above 50%.
